This appeal is filed against the order dated 16.07.2022 passed on I.A.No.1 in O.S.No.5059/2021, on the file of the XIX Additional City Civil and Sessions Judge, Bangalore, rejecting I.A.No.1 filed under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 read with Section 151 of CPC, wherein a prayer was made to grant temporary injunction restraining the defendant from interfering with the peaceful possession and enjoyment of the suit schedule property and also from interfering with the construction on the schedule site.

entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: 2. The factual matrix of the case of the plaintiff in a suit for permanent injunction is that the plaintiff is in settled possession over the suit schedule property, which is a part of residential layout formed by REMCO (BHEL) House Building Co- operative Society Ltd. ("REMCO Society" for short) for the benefit of employees of BHEL; a public sector undertaking of the Government of India.

entities.text: REMCO (BHEL) House Building Co- operative Society Ltd.
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: One such employee by name B.N.Ramesh, who was allotted the suit schedule property and a conveyance was executed in his favour by the Society on 26.04.1997.
Hence, he has been put in possession.
The residential layout has been formed on several survey numbers and the layout is fully formed.
So, the land completely lost its original character and it is now having all civic amenities.
The allottee of REMCO Society got constructed their respective houses and some of them got constructed compound walls to protect their sites.
So, the REMCO Society and its allottees were in settled possession of the sites and even B.N. Ramesh was also in settled possession since 1997.

3. It is contended by the plaintiff that the plaintiff purchased the suit property from the defendant for a valuable consideration on 25.10.2018 and during purchase, the shed was in existence with electricity supply, water and sanitary connections.
The khatha has been changed in her name and she is also paying water bills and electricity bills since from the date of purchase.
She obtained building licence from BBMP for construction of residential house and accordingly commenced the construction on 13.08.2021 by sinking bore well.
During that point of time, the defendant approached with the police to the suit property and made an enquiry.
So, her husband produced all the documents to the police.
The police officials having been satisfied with the said documents, did not interfere.

But on 27.08.2021 around 11 a.m., the defendant with his 15 to 20 henchmen arrived to the suit property and physically pulled the shed and threatened the plaintiff with dire consequences and also attempted to demolish the entire shed.
So, she filed the criminal complaint with the jurisdictional police.
The defendant without there being any authority of law was disturbing her possession over the suit property.

Hence, she was constrained to file the present suit for permanent injunction restraining the defendant from interfering with the peaceful possession of the suit schedule property of the plaintiff and construction, which has been undertaken by the plaintiff and also sought for temporary injunction against the defendant.

sentences.text: The learned counsel brought to the notice of this Court paragraph No.12 of the judgment, wherein it is discussed with regard to Section 49 and the proviso provides that any document which is required to be registered, if not registered, shall not affect any immovable property comprised therein nor such document shall be received as evidence of any transaction affecting such property.

The proviso, however, would show that an unregistered document affecting immovable property and required by the 1908 Act or the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 to be registered may be received as an evidence to the contract in a suit for specific performance or as evidence of any collateral transaction not required to be effected by registered instrument.

sentences.text: The learned counsel referring these documents would vehemently contend that the defendant claims right in respect of the suit schedule property in terms of the sale deed executed in his favour and also other documents.
The learned counsel relies upon the judgments of this Court passed in M.F.A.No.7776/2015 and M.F.A.No.722/2021, wherein the appeal is dismissed in a similar set of facts and circumstances.

The learned counsel relied upon the judgment of the Apex Court in the case of Anathula Sudhakar (supra) contending that when dispute is with regard to title is concerned, the suit itself is not maintainable for the relief of bare injunction.

The learned counsel also relied upon the Apex Court judgment in the case of Madan Gopal Rungta (supra), wherein it is held that for any other purpose, meaning of interim relief without decision on rights, if any order has been passed.
20. The learned counsel relying upon these judgments would contend that the appeal itself is devoid of merits and the same requires to be dismissed.

21. Having heard the learned counsel for the appellant and the learned counsel for the respondent and keeping in view the principles laid in the judgments referred supra by the learned counsel for the appellant and the learned counsel for the respondent, this Court has to examine whether the Trial Court committed an error in dismissing the application.
Admittedly, there was an acquisition in respect of the suit schedule property and the same has been questioned and this Court quashed the acquisition proceedings.
The same was challenged before the Apex Court and the Apex Court also confirmed the same and a direction was given to deliver the possession in favour of the original owners.
It is not in dispute that the order to refund, if any compensation is awarded, was passed.

It is important to note that the Trial Court has taken note of the same in paragraph No.15 with regard to acquisition and quashing of the proceedings, particularly in different survey numbers in paragraph No.16 and also the order of the Supreme Court was noted and also taken note of a direction has been given for restoring the possession to the land owners and the said land owners shall refund the amount so received by them as compensation.
It is important to note that the endorsement issued by BDA also taken note that there is no layout formed by REMCO Society.

It is important to note that consequent upon the order passed by the Apex Court, the Government of Karnataka issued notice dated 18.04.1998 and also similar notice dated 30.09.2002 in order to implement the order of the Apex Court and property was also restored to the land owners.

It is important to note that REMCO Society executed the indemnity bond on 23.04.2004 in favour of the Government of Karnataka to receive the deposited amount of Rs.36,21,794/-, which was disputed by the Society towards land cost in respect of acquisition since the acquisition proceedings was quashed by the Apex Court and the same was noted in paragraph No.18.

On the other hand, the Trial Court taken note of the claim made by the defendant with regard to acquisition of property by the vendor of the defendant vide gift deed dated 07.11.2015 and execution of registered sale deed dated 11.11.2020.

The learned counsel for the appellant in his written arguments relying upon the document of registered sale deed executed by the vendor i.e., Anjanappa and others in favour of Mirle Varadaraj,
document No.11 referred by the defendant contended that bogus documents are created and conversion is also subsequent to the sale made and the same is obtained by the original owners and also taken note of document of registered gift deed dated 07.11.2015, which has been claimed by wife of Mirle Varadaraj and contend that khatha certificate and khatha extracts are obtained fraudulently and RTI information also collected and the same is produced under an application under Order 41 Rule 27 of CPC and the said properties are in respect of the defendant claim is concerned and so also earlier suit filed and R.F.A. filed, wherein compromise was entered.
It is also the contention of the plaintiff that a document of confirmation was also executed and admittedly the said document is an unregistered document.

The learned counsel for the appellant brought to the notice of this Court the judgment of the Apex Court in the case of S.Kaladevi (supra), wherein it is discussed with regard to Section 49 that is in respect of consideration of unregistered sale deed of an immovable property of the value of Rs.100/- and more could be admitted in evidence as evidence of contract in a suit for specific performance of contract.

Here is a case with regard to the title in concerned, since the plaintiff claims right based on the earlier sale deed executed by the Society and subsequent confirmation and hence Kaladevi's case will not come to the aid of the appellant.

23. The learned counsel relied upon the judgment of the Apex Court in the case of Sunkamma (supra), wherein it is held that the plaintiff is only required to prove that he is in lawful possession of suit property, as the touchstone upon which such suit has to be decided is "lawful possession" and not "ownership".

In the case on hand, it has to be noted that admittedly the properties are acquired and the same was quashed and a direction was given by the Apex Court to re- deliver the possession in favour of the owners and the same has been acted upon by issuing notice to the respective properties and re-delivery of possession is also placed on record.
When such being the case, the unregistered document of confirmation deed, relied upon by the plaintiff, will not convey any right.

24. The documents are also produced before this Court by filing an application under Order 41 Rule 27 of CPC and those documents, particularly proceedings of the Joint Commissioner of BBMP,
registered sale deed dated 20.07.2011, copies of khatha extract, are all with regard to the payment of tax is concerned.

No doubt, the plaintiff also produced some of the tax paid receipts and disputing the documents of the defendant with regard to the issuance of the khatha certificate and endorsement is also issued by the concerned authority that and no such endorsements are issued.

These are the documents which can be relied upon during the course of trial and the additional documents which have been produced before the Court will not come to the aid of the appellant while considering the application filed under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of CPC.
Admittedly, the property which was acquired was quashed and direction was given by the Apex Court confirming the quashing of the proceedings.
When such direction was given by the Apex Court, the concerned authorities have also acted upon.
The plaintiff has to make out the case not by alleging about the documents of the defendant that those documents are bogus documents.

When the possession was delivered in favour of the original owners, the very contention of the plaintiff that the plaintiff has been in possession of the property is the subject matter of trial and the same cannot be decided in an application filed under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of CPC.
The plaintiff has to make out a prima facie case and in an application of interlocutory, the Court cannot express any opinion on merits.

sentences.text: The Trial Court taking note of the order passed by this Court in W.P.No.21920/2010 and other connected matters for revocation of khatha is concerned, rightly comes to the conclusion that the same is not helpful to the case of the plaintiff and considered the dismissal of M.F.A.No.7776/2015 and M.F.A.No.722/2021.
No doubt, other orders are also before the Court and the same has been challenged before the Apex Court and the order has been passed to maintain status quo.

In the case of hand, the specific contention is taken by the plaintiff that she had purchased the property in 2018 and admittedly, structure which was in existence has already been demolished as admittedly by the plaintiff.
It is also the contention of the plaintiff that the defendant is causing obstruction in the construction.

When the plaintiff has not made out a prima facie case to grant the relief of temporary injunction and no balance of convenience in favour of the plaintiff and with regard to the claim is concerned, the matter has to be determined by the Trial Court.

It is important to note that the suit is filed for the relief of permanent injunction and when the very title is disputed and when there is a cloud on the title, there is a force in the contention of the learned counsel for the respondent.

The learned counsel for the respondent relied upon the judgment of the Apex Court in the case of Anathula Sudhakar (supra), wherein the Apex Court observed that when the title is in dispute and when there is a cloud on the title, the suit for comprehensive suit is appropriate remedy and only where the title is not disputed or under a cloud, but is out of possession, then the remedy is suit for possession with consequential injunction.

It is the contention of the plaintiff that the plaintiff is in lawful possession and the same is disputed and the defendant is also claiming that he has been in possession relying upon the sale deed as well as khatha certificate and other documents.
When there is a cloud on the title and the suit is for bare injunction, I am of the opinion that it is not a fit case to reverse the finding of the Trial Court.
The Trial Court has considered the material on record and passed a reasoned order and the same does not require any interference of this Court.

26. In view of the discussions made above, I pass the following:
ORDER
The appeal is dismissed.

Consequently, I.A. filed under Order 41 Rule 27 (aa)
read with Section 151 of CPC, is disposed of as observed above.
